But those feelings definitely flare up most intensely when I'm forced to sit still for long exams, wait in lines, or when I impulsively interrupt people in conversations.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to manage your inattention symptoms, such as with the help of deadlines or highly engaging tasks, do your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms remain as problematic, or do they seem to decrease in intensity?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure if they actually decrease or stay the same. Even when I'm hyper-focused on a last-minute deadline, I still feel really physically restless and find myself constantly fidgeting. It's hard to tell if the overall intensity changes in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you're able to control your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms effectively, but still struggle significantly with inattention and disorganization, or vice versa?\n\nPatient: Yes, during a long exam or a three-hour lab, I'll force myself to sit still and look calm on the outside so I don't disrupt others, but internally I still feel a buzzing restlessness. Even though I'm managing the physical hyperactivity in those moments, my attention completely fails me, leading to careless errors like misreading a column name or missing a minus sign on the test.\n\nDoctor: Looking back at your experiences, do you think there was ever a time when your symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks, were significantly more prominent than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or have they always been roughly equal in impact?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really compared them that way before. Both the focus issues and the restlessness or fidgeting feel like they have always been there together since I was a kid. Because of that, it's really hard to say if one was ever significantly more prominent than the other.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your childhood, did you exhibit more symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as fidgeting and interrupting, or more symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks or being easily distracted?\n\nPatient: I actually had a pretty even mix of both when I was younger. My teachers used to write that I was \"bright but daydreams\" and would rush or forget to hand in homework I'd already finished, while my parents got called in because I was constantly fidgeting in my seat and blurting out answers.\n\nDoctor: In your daily life, are there specific situations or environments where one set of symptoms, either inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity, clearly overshadows the other, or do they consistently co-occur?\n\nPatient: They definitely show up differently depending on the environment. In academic settings like coding or lectures, my inattention, distractibility, and internal physical restlessness are what really take over. But in social settings, group projects, or when I'm trying to relax at home, the hyperactivity and impulsivity like pacing and interrupting others become much more dominant.\n\nDoctor: Considering your entire life, including childhood and now, do you think the symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through, or the symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting, have been more persistent or problematic for you overall?\n\nPatient: Both have been constant since I was a kid, but they've impacted me differently at different stages of my life. When I was younger, the hyperactivity and impulsivity, like my fidgeting and blurting things out, were what teachers and parents noticed most. Now that I'm in college, the inattention and struggle to follow through on projects are definitely the most problematic and destructive to my life, even though that internal buzzing restlessness is still very much there.\n\nDoctor: Looking back, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity have been relatively balanced throughout your life, or has one set of symptoms become more prominent as you've grown older?\n\nPatient: Both have been present since childhood, back when teachers noted my daydreaming and my parents got called in for my fidgeting and blurting out answers. However, over the last year and a half, the inattention has felt much more prominent and unmanageable due to the intense focus and planning required for my data science courses. The hyperactivity is still very much there, but it has shifted from childhood behaviors into a constant internal restlessness and fidgeting.\n\nDoctor: When considering the impact on your daily life and relationships, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following through on tasks, are slightly more problematic than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or are they equally troublesome?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure which one is worse, and I haven't thought about it that way. Both the focus issues and the constant restlessness feel very disruptive to my daily life, just in completely different ways.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was ever a distinct period in your life where you felt that either your inattention symptoms or your hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms were clearly more severe or troublesome than the other, even if it was just for a short time?"
  }

Even when I try to do relaxing things like reading or sketching, I get so uncomfortable that I start humming, talking to myself, or constantly checking my phone. It's really hard for me to just be quiet and still.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your difficulty with following through on tasks and getting distracted is more due to not being able to focus or because you're getting bored and looking for something more stimulating or exciting to do?\n\nPatient: It's honestly a combination of both. I'll get super excited about a new project and do the fun parts, but then I stall out and get bored once that initial spark is gone. At the same time, even when I am trying to focus, my brain just drifts off or I get completely derailed by tiny distractions like a Slack notification or a random thought.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself taking unnecessary risks or doing things impulsively, like spending money recklessly or driving recklessly, without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience those specific behaviors. I've never really had issues with reckless spending or dangerous driving, so that hasn't been a problem for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms are more related to problems with inattention and disorganization, or do you also experience significant hyperactivity-impulsivity issues that affect your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: I’d say it’s definitely a mix of both. While the inattention and disorganization really hurt my school and freelance work by causing me to stall out and miss deadlines, the hyperactivity and impulsivity are just as bad, especially with my constant physical restlessness, fidgeting, and tendency to interrupt people during group projects.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following through on tasks, and your symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting others, compare in terms of which ones cause you the most trouble or are most noticeable to you and others?\n\nPatient: The inattention symptoms definitely cause me the most severe practical trouble, since failing to follow through and missing deadlines is actively threatening my grades and my freelance career. But the hyperactivity and impulsivity are definitely what's most outwardly noticeable to others, like my roommates joking that I can't chill, people noticing my constant leg bouncing, and me interrupting people during conversations.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your difficulties with inattention, such as not following through on tasks, are more prominent than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or are they roughly equal in how much they affect your daily life?\n\nPatient: They feel pretty equal overall, just in different areas of my life. The inattention and lack of follow-through really damage my academic and freelance work, while the physical restlessness, constant pacing, and interrupting people affect my daily physical comfort and my social relationships.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms affect you, but can you estimate roughly what percentage of your daily struggles you'd attribute to each, to help clarify which might be more predominant?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of an exact percentage because both the focus issues and the restlessness feel constantly present and intertwined in my daily life. They happen at the same time so much that it's really hard for me to separate or quantify them.\n\nDoctor: When you're in situations where you can focus on a task without distractions, do you still experience significant restlessness or impulsivity, or do these symptoms primarily emerge when you're trying to focus or wait your turn?\n\nPatient: I actually experience restlessness in both situations. Even during quiet, relaxing tasks like sketching, I feel uncomfortable and end up humming or pacing around. But those feelings definitely flare up most intensely when I'm forced to sit still for long exams, wait in lines, or when I impulsively interrupt people in conversations.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to manage your inattention symptoms, such as with the help of deadlines or highly engaging tasks, do your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms remain as problematic, or do they seem to decrease in intensity?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure if they actually decrease or stay the same. Even when I'm hyper-focused on a last-minute deadline, I still feel really physically restless and find myself constantly fidgeting. It's hard to tell if the overall intensity changes in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you're able to control your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms effectively, but still struggle significantly with inattention and disorganization, or vice versa?\n\nPatient: Yes, during a long exam or a three-hour lab, I'll force myself to sit still and look calm on the outside so I don't disrupt others, but internally I still feel a buzzing restlessness. Even though I'm managing the physical hyperactivity in those moments, my attention completely fails me, leading to careless errors like misreading a column name or missing a minus sign on the test.\n\nDoctor: Looking back at your experiences, do you think there was ever a time when your symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks, were significantly more prominent than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or have they always been roughly equal in impact?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really compared them that way before. Both the focus issues and the restlessness or fidgeting feel like they have always been there together since I was a kid. Because of that, it's really hard to say if one was ever significantly more prominent than the other.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your childhood, did you exhibit more symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as fidgeting and interrupting, or more symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks or being easily distracted?\n\nPatient: I actually had a pretty even mix of both when I was younger. My teachers used to write that I was \"bright but daydreams\" and would rush or forget to hand in homework I'd already finished, while my parents got called in because I was constantly fidgeting in my seat and blurting out answers.\n\nDoctor: In your daily life, are there specific situations or environments where one set of symptoms, either inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity, clearly overshadows the other, or do they consistently co-occur?\n\nPatient: They definitely show up differently depending on the environment. In academic settings like coding or lectures, my inattention, distractibility, and internal physical restlessness are what really take over. But in social settings, group projects, or when I'm trying to relax at home, the hyperactivity and impulsivity like pacing and interrupting others become much more dominant.\n\nDoctor: Considering your entire life, including childhood and now, do you think the symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through, or the symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting, have been more persistent or problematic for you overall?\n\nPatient: Both have been constant since I was a kid, but they've impacted me differently at different stages of my life. When I was younger, the hyperactivity and impulsivity, like my fidgeting and blurting things out, were what teachers and parents noticed most. Now that I'm in college, the inattention and struggle to follow through on projects are definitely the most problematic and destructive to my life, even though that internal buzzing restlessness is still very much there.\n\nDoctor: Looking back, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity have been relatively balanced throughout your life, or has one set of symptoms become more prominent as you've grown older?\n\nPatient: Both have been present since childhood, back when teachers noted my daydreaming and my parents got called in for my fidgeting and blurting out answers. However, over the last year and a half, the inattention has felt much more prominent and unmanageable due to the intense focus and planning required for my data science courses. The hyperactivity is still very much there, but it has shifted from childhood behaviors into a constant internal restlessness and fidgeting.\n\nDoctor: When considering the impact on your daily life and relationships, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following through on tasks, are slightly more problematic than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or are they equally troublesome?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure which one is worse, and I haven't thought about it that way. Both the focus issues and the constant restlessness feel very disruptive to my daily life, just in completely different ways.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was ever a distinct period in your life where you felt that either your inattention symptoms or your hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms were clearly more severe or troublesome than the other, even if it was just for a short time?\n\nPatient: I can't really recall a specific period where one was worse than the other. Both the focus issues and the restlessness have always seemed to go hand-in-hand for me since childhood, and they've always felt equally troublesome. They just feel like they've constantly been tangled together.\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing significant stress or pressure, do you find that your symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity become more pronounced, and if so, which set of symptoms tends to worsen first?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure which specific set of symptoms worsens first when I'm stressed. Both my focus issues and my restlessness seem to feed into each other and get worse together when I'm under pressure.\n\nDoctor: Looking at your overall life, do you think the difficulties with inattention, such as not following through on tasks, or the symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting others, have been more persistent or equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: They have been equally problematic and persistent throughout my entire life. Looking back to childhood, I struggled with both sides, like daydreaming and forgetting homework alongside constant fidgeting and blurting out answers. Even now, the focus issues and the physical restlessness or interrupting feel like constant, intertwined challenges.\n\nDoctor: In your current daily life, are there any situations where you can effectively manage one set of symptoms, either inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity, but still struggle significantly with the other?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed a situation where I can successfully manage one set of symptoms while struggling with the other. For me, both the inattention and the restlessness tend to occur together and feel equally hard to control at the same time.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific times of the day when you notice that either your inattention symptoms or your hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms are worse, or do they tend to remain relatively consistent throughout the day?"

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I haven't really noticed a specific pattern or time of day when things are worse. They feel pretty consistent from morning to night, and it usually just depends on how engaging or difficult the task is rather than the time of day.

It's really starting to impact my grades and my career, and I feel like I'm constantly scrambling.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself getting distracted by new ideas or activities, or having trouble waiting for your turn, like interrupting others or blurting out answers?\n\nPatient: Yes, I struggle with both of those a lot. I get pulled off task by the tiniest distractions and constantly start new side projects, and I also get really impatient waiting in lines or for my turn to speak. I frequently catch myself cutting people off and interrupting during group projects before they can even finish their sentences.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have difficulty engaging in quiet leisure activities, like reading or watching a movie, without getting up to do something else?\n\nPatient: Yes, completely—I'm always bouncing my leg, clicking pens, or picking at my notebook, and sitting still for too long gives me this buzzing feeling under my skin like I'm going to crawl out of it. Even when I try to do relaxing things like reading or sketching, I get so uncomfortable that I start humming, talking to myself, or constantly checking my phone. It's really hard for me to just be quiet and still.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your difficulty with following through on tasks and getting distracted is more due to not being able to focus or because you're getting bored and looking for something more stimulating or exciting to do?\n\nPatient: It's honestly a combination of both. I'll get super excited about a new project and do the fun parts, but then I stall out and get bored once that initial spark is gone. At the same time, even when I am trying to focus, my brain just drifts off or I get completely derailed by tiny distractions like a Slack notification or a random thought.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself taking unnecessary risks or doing things impulsively, like spending money recklessly or driving recklessly, without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience those specific behaviors. I've never really had issues with reckless spending or dangerous driving, so that hasn't been a problem for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your symptoms are more related to problems with inattention and disorganization, or do you also experience significant hyperactivity-impulsivity issues that affect your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: I’d say it’s definitely a mix of both. While the inattention and disorganization really hurt my school and freelance work by causing me to stall out and miss deadlines, the hyperactivity and impulsivity are just as bad, especially with my constant physical restlessness, fidgeting, and tendency to interrupt people during group projects.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following through on tasks, and your symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting others, compare in terms of which ones cause you the most trouble or are most noticeable to you and others?\n\nPatient: The inattention symptoms definitely cause me the most severe practical trouble, since failing to follow through and missing deadlines is actively threatening my grades and my freelance career. But the hyperactivity and impulsivity are definitely what's most outwardly noticeable to others, like my roommates joking that I can't chill, people noticing my constant leg bouncing, and me interrupting people during conversations.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your difficulties with inattention, such as not following through on tasks, are more prominent than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or are they roughly equal in how much they affect your daily life?\n\nPatient: They feel pretty equal overall, just in different areas of my life. The inattention and lack of follow-through really damage my academic and freelance work, while the physical restlessness, constant pacing, and interrupting people affect my daily physical comfort and my social relationships.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms affect you, but can you estimate roughly what percentage of your daily struggles you'd attribute to each, to help clarify which might be more predominant?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of an exact percentage because both the focus issues and the restlessness feel constantly present and intertwined in my daily life. They happen at the same time so much that it's really hard for me to separate or quantify them.\n\nDoctor: When you're in situations where you can focus on a task without distractions, do you still experience significant restlessness or impulsivity, or do these symptoms primarily emerge when you're trying to focus or wait your turn?\n\nPatient: I actually experience restlessness in both situations. Even during quiet, relaxing tasks like sketching, I feel uncomfortable and end up humming or pacing around. But those feelings definitely flare up most intensely when I'm forced to sit still for long exams, wait in lines, or when I impulsively interrupt people in conversations.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to manage your inattention symptoms, such as with the help of deadlines or highly engaging tasks, do your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms remain as problematic, or do they seem to decrease in intensity?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure if they actually decrease or stay the same. Even when I'm hyper-focused on a last-minute deadline, I still feel really physically restless and find myself constantly fidgeting. It's hard to tell if the overall intensity changes in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you're able to control your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms effectively, but still struggle significantly with inattention and disorganization, or vice versa?\n\nPatient: Yes, during a long exam or a three-hour lab, I'll force myself to sit still and look calm on the outside so I don't disrupt others, but internally I still feel a buzzing restlessness. Even though I'm managing the physical hyperactivity in those moments, my attention completely fails me, leading to careless errors like misreading a column name or missing a minus sign on the test.\n\nDoctor: Looking back at your experiences, do you think there was ever a time when your symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks, were significantly more prominent than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or have they always been roughly equal in impact?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really compared them that way before. Both the focus issues and the restlessness or fidgeting feel like they have always been there together since I was a kid. Because of that, it's really hard to say if one was ever significantly more prominent than the other.\n\nDoctor: When you think about your childhood, did you exhibit more symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as fidgeting and interrupting, or more symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through on tasks or being easily distracted?\n\nPatient: I actually had a pretty even mix of both when I was younger. My teachers used to write that I was \"bright but daydreams\" and would rush or forget to hand in homework I'd already finished, while my parents got called in because I was constantly fidgeting in my seat and blurting out answers.\n\nDoctor: In your daily life, are there specific situations or environments where one set of symptoms, either inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity, clearly overshadows the other, or do they consistently co-occur?\n\nPatient: They definitely show up differently depending on the environment. In academic settings like coding or lectures, my inattention, distractibility, and internal physical restlessness are what really take over. But in social settings, group projects, or when I'm trying to relax at home, the hyperactivity and impulsivity like pacing and interrupting others become much more dominant.\n\nDoctor: Considering your entire life, including childhood and now, do you think the symptoms of inattention, like difficulty following through, or the symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting, have been more persistent or problematic for you overall?\n\nPatient: Both have been constant since I was a kid, but they've impacted me differently at different stages of my life. When I was younger, the hyperactivity and impulsivity, like my fidgeting and blurting things out, were what teachers and parents noticed most. Now that I'm in college, the inattention and struggle to follow through on projects are definitely the most problematic and destructive to my life, even though that internal buzzing restlessness is still very much there.\n\nDoctor: Looking back, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity have been relatively balanced throughout your life, or has one set of symptoms become more prominent as you've grown older?\n\nPatient: Both have been present since childhood, back when teachers noted my daydreaming and my parents got called in for my fidgeting and blurting out answers. However, over the last year and a half, the inattention has felt much more prominent and unmanageable due to the intense focus and planning required for my data science courses. The hyperactivity is still very much there, but it has shifted from childhood behaviors into a constant internal restlessness and fidgeting.\n\nDoctor: When considering the impact on your daily life and relationships, do you feel that your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following through on tasks, are slightly more problematic than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, or are they equally troublesome?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure which one is worse, and I haven't thought about it that way. Both the focus issues and the constant restlessness feel very disruptive to my daily life, just in completely different ways.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was ever a distinct period in your life where you felt that either your inattention symptoms or your hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms were clearly more severe or troublesome than the other, even if it was just for a short time?\n\nPatient: I can't really recall a specific period where one was worse than the other. Both the focus issues and the restlessness have always seemed to go hand-in-hand for me since childhood, and they've always felt equally troublesome. They just feel like they've constantly been tangled together.\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing significant stress or pressure, do you find that your symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity become more pronounced, and if so, which set of symptoms tends to worsen first?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure which specific set of symptoms worsens first when I'm stressed. Both my focus issues and my restlessness seem to feed into each other and get worse together when I'm under pressure.\n\nDoctor: Looking at your overall life, do you think the difficulties with inattention, such as not following through on tasks, or the symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, like restlessness and interrupting others, have been more persistent or equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: They have been equally problematic and persistent throughout my entire life. Looking back to childhood, I struggled with both sides, like daydreaming and forgetting homework alongside constant fidgeting and blurting out answers. Both the focus issues and the physical restlessness have felt constantly challenging and unmanageable over the last year and a half.
